title: Area IX review: Emergency Operations
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area IX: emergency descents, emergency approach and landing, system and equipment malfunctions, and emergency equipment and survival gear. Many link two Tasks, like a cabin fire that leads to an emergency descent.

questions.q: You are making a long power-off descent on a humid 60 °F day in a carbureted trainer. The engine runs rough, then quits. Which critical item is most likely to bring the power back?
options: Mixture to full lean
Magneto switch to OFF
Carburetor heat to full ON
Master switch to OFF
questions.why: Carburetor heat is one of the critical items to check after an engine failure [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Carburetor ice is most dangerous at reduced power in a descent, and the fix is full heat, left on until normal power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Full lean or magnetos OFF would stop the engine, not restart it.

questions.q: Look at the table. Your alternator fails at night while the landing lights and the heater blower motor are both on. About how much current are those two items drawing from the battery?
options: About 31.8 amps
About 3.8 amps
About 14 amps
About 17.8 amps
questions.why: The table lists 17.80 amps for the landing lights and 14.00 amps for the heater blower: 17.80 + 14.00 = 31.80 amps [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. That is close to the 40-amp load the AFH says might drain a battery in about 10 or 15 minutes, so shed non-essential loads right away [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

questions.q: Your retractable airplane has VNE 175 knots, VLE 140 knots and VFE 110 knots. For the emergency descent the POH says gear down, flaps up, and you target the maximum allowable airspeed. The air is smooth. Which steady airspeed meets the ACS standard?
options: 144 knots
136 knots
127 knots
112 knots
questions.why: With the gear down, VLE (140 knots) is the limit, so it is the maximum allowable airspeed [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The ACS allows the appropriate airspeed +0/-10 knots, so 130 to 140 knots passes. 144 knots exceeds VLE, and 127 and 112 knots are more than 10 knots slow.

questions.q: Your ELT transmitted for 25 minutes during a false alarm last year and for 40 minutes during a search exercise this month. Both happened on its current battery, which is well within its useful life. What does 14 CFR 91.207 require?
options: Nothing yet, because neither use lasted more than 1 hour
Nothing until the next 12-month inspection
Replace the battery only if it fails a ground test
Replace or recharge the battery, because it has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour
questions.why: The battery must be replaced (or recharged) when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour. 25 + 40 = 65 minutes, which is more than 1 hour in total [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

questions.q: You climb through rain near freezing with pitch and power unchanged. The airspeed indicator keeps rising as you climb, and it drops when you descend. The altimeter and VSI look normal. What is the likely cause?
options: The static port is blocked
The pitot tube and its drain hole are both blocked
Only the pitot tube is blocked and its drain hole is open
The vacuum pump has failed
questions.why: With the pitot tube and drain hole both clogged, pressure is trapped in the pitot line, so the airspeed indicator reads higher as you climb and lower as you descend, like an altimeter [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. If the drain hole were open, the airspeed would drop to zero. A blocked static port would also freeze the altimeter and VSI [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

questions.q: Your engine quits in cruise. The left tank is selected and its gauge shows 10 gallons. What does the AFH suggest about the fuel selector?
options: Consider switching to the other tank anyway, because fuel gauges can be inaccurate
Leave it alone, since the gauge shows fuel in that tank
Turn it OFF to prevent a fire before landing
Switch only after the field is made, to save time
questions.why: Many real emergency landings were caused by a fuel selector set to an empty tank. The AFH says it may be wise to change the selector position even if the gauge shows fuel, because gauges can be inaccurate [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

questions.q: You are flying a pressurized airplane when the cabin suddenly loses pressure at high altitude. According to the PHAK, what must you do quickly?
options: Hold altitude and troubleshoot the pressurization system first
Slow to best glide speed and descend gently
Turn off the master switch and descend at VA
Use oxygen right away and make a rapid descent
questions.why: The main danger of decompression is hypoxia, so quick use of oxygen is needed to avoid unconsciousness, and a rapid descent is needed [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. A sudden loss of cabin pressurization is one of the reasons for an emergency descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: Your airplane's ELT is broken and you are at a remote strip with no repair shop. A friend wants to ride along to the shop 80 NM away. What does 14 CFR 91.207 allow?
options: You may ferry it with your friend aboard, since it is a one-time flight
The airplane may not fly at all until a mechanic comes to the strip
You may ferry it to the shop, but only required crewmembers may be aboard, so your friend cannot come
You may fly with your friend aboard if you stay within 50 NM
questions.why: You may ferry an airplane with an inoperative ELT from a place where it can't be repaired to a place where it can, but no one other than required crewmembers may be carried [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]]. The 50 NM exception covers only training operations conducted entirely within 50 NM of the airport where they began, not a trip with a passenger [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

questions.q: In cruise the electric trim starts running nose down by itself, and the control forces build fast. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Press the trim disconnect if installed, or pull the trim circuit breaker, then hold pitch by hand
Turn the battery master off and on again to reset the trim
Add full flaps to balance the nose-down trim
Keep pressing the trim switch nose up until it stops
questions.why: For a trim runaway, quickly assess it, then press the trim disconnect (if installed) or pull the trim power circuit breaker. Depending on the control forces, you may need a no-flap landing because of the flap pitching moments [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

questions.q: On the checkride you fly an emergency descent with a target of 115 knots, and later a simulated engine failure where your POH best glide is 70 knots. Which pair of steady airspeeds meets both ACS standards?
options: Descent 118 knots, glide 72 knots
Descent 103 knots, glide 66 knots
Descent 111 knots, glide 81 knots
Descent 108 knots, glide 79 knots
questions.why: The emergency descent allows +0/-10 knots (105 to 115), because going faster risks the limit speeds [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Best glide allows ±10 knots (60 to 80). Only 108 and 79 fit both. 118 is too fast for the descent, 103 is too slow, and 81 is too fast for the glide. Holding best glide gives the most distance per altitude lost [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

questions.q: A radio starts smoking. You pull its circuit breaker, but you can still see small flames behind the panel. What should you do?
options: Do nothing more, since removing power always puts out an electrical fire
Use the fire extinguisher, since materials that caught fire can keep burning after power is removed
Open the cabin vents first, then use the extinguisher
Reset the breaker to find out which circuit failed
questions.why: Even after the faulty circuit is shut off, materials that have been ignited may continue to burn [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to clear smoke, and land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: You start an emergency descent in a fixed-gear trainer with the flaps up and hit moderate turbulence. The POH lists VA 105 knots for your current weight, VNO 127 knots, VNE 160 knots and VFE 85 knots. What is your upper airspeed limit?
options: 160 knots
127 knots
105 knots
85 knots
questions.why: In turbulence you must also comply with VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]], the most speed at which gusts or full control deflection won't cause structural damage [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. VNO and VNE are higher, and VNO is for smooth air only [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. VFE does not apply because the flaps are up.

questions.q: You suspect a partly blocked static system. How does the AFH say to confirm it?
options: Open the alternate static source in level flight and watch the airspeed only
Turn on pitot heat and wait for the altimeter to unfreeze
Tap the altimeter and compare it with the attitude indicator
Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending; if the needles move a lot, use it for the rest of the flight
questions.why: Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending. If the needles move significantly, a static problem exists, so keep using the alternate source [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Cabin static pressure is lower than outside, so check the POH for corrections [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

questions.q: Your engine quits at 7,000 feet AGL, right above a long, open field you can easily reach. You want as much time as possible to troubleshoot and talk to ATC. Which speed fits best?
options: Minimum sink speed, a few knots slower than best glide
Best glide speed, because it keeps you aloft longest
A speed well above best glide, to keep the engine windmilling
The slowest speed you can hold without a stall warning
questions.why: Minimum sink speed loses altitude at the lowest rate, so it gives the most time in the air, at the cost of distance. It is generally a few knots below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Best glide gives the most distance, not the most time [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

questions.q: You file one VFR flight plan for a trip with two en route stops, with an ETE to your final destination (ETA 1700). You go down on the first leg at 1000 and can't call anyone. Unless other information comes in, when would someone probably start looking for you?
options: Around 1030, as soon as radar loses you
About 36 hours later, when family notices
Around 1730, 30 minutes after your ETA at the final destination
Around 1130, 30 minutes after you should have reached the first stop
questions.why: With a long flight plan that has several stops, a mishap could happen on any leg, and it is probable no one would start looking until 30 minutes after your ETA at the final destination. For best protection, file only to the first landing and refile for each leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. The 36 hours applies to pilots with no flight plan [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

questions.q: Your landing gear won't extend by the normal or the alternate method in the POH. What does the AFH recommend?
options: Land on the nearest rough grass strip, because it causes fewer sparks
Plan a gear-up landing at an airport with crash and rescue, ask for emergency equipment, and consider burning off fuel
Keep cycling the gear until it works, even if fuel runs low
Dive and pull up hard to force the gear down
questions.why: Once the gear won't respond to normal or alternate extension, plan a gear-up landing. Pick an airport with crash and rescue if possible, ask for emergency equipment to stand by, and consider burning off excess fuel to lower landing speed and fire risk. A smooth hard runway usually causes less damage than rough grass [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

questions.q: Smoke and a burning-insulation smell fill the cabin. You can't find the bad circuit, so you plan to turn the master switch off and start an emergency descent. Why make your distress call before you switch it off?
options: With the master off, you can't transmit, and ATC loses your transponder return
The master switch also shuts off the engine
ATC requires a call before any descent below cruise altitude
Turning the master off resets the transponder to 7700
questions.why: If you can't find and isolate the faulty circuit, turn off the battery master and alternator if flight conditions permit [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. That shuts off the panel radios for distress calls and makes ATC lose your transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

questions.q: You are a VFR pilot without an instrument rating. You are lost and low on fuel, and a radar controller is giving you vectors. The vectors are about to take you into clouds. What does the AIM say?
options: Follow the vectors exactly, since ATC is now responsible for your safety
Turn off your transponder so ATC can't vector you into clouds
Accept the clouds, since radar vectors allow you to break the regulations
Choose a course that keeps you in VFR conditions if one exists; the vectors are advice, and safe flight is still up to you
questions.why: Radar vectors for a VFR pilot in difficulty are advisory; responsibility for flying safely stays with the pilot, and they don't permit you to violate the regulations. If a course that keeps you in VFR conditions is available, a pilot without an instrument rating should choose it rather than a vector into IFR weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

questions.q: In a glass-cockpit trainer, both the PFD and MFD go dark and won't come back. Which instruments are you left with?
options: Only the magnetic compass
The turn coordinator and VSI
The standby attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and magnetic compass
A backup moving map on the MFD in reversionary mode
questions.why: Aircraft with electronic displays have a standby attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and magnetic compass for use when the PFD is unavailable. These would be the only instruments left [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

questions.q: You and a passenger ride down under the airplane's ballistic parachute into a field. The surface wind is gusty. What does the AFH say about this moment?
options: The parachute holds the airplane in place, so wait inside for rescuers
The deployed parachute and the surface wind create hazards, so everyone should know how to get out
The airplane can be flown out once the parachute is cut away
Surface wind no longer matters once the wheels touch the ground
questions.why: Once on the ground, a deployed parachute and the surface wind create hazards, and the occupants should know the evacuation procedures. Deployment usually means the airframe is lost [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

questions.q: During an emergency descent for cabin smoke, you stare at the smoke source behind the panel while the airspeed creeps toward the red line. What does this show?
options: Smoke always means the airspeed indicator has failed
Fixation is helpful because it finds the fire faster
Airspeed doesn't matter during an emergency descent
Fixating on one problem pushed out more important tasks; stop, think, slow down and prioritize
questions.why: When a pilot fixates on one problem, the unnecessary focus pushes out tasks of greater importance [[24:51|AFH 2-14]], like keeping the speed below VNE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. In a work overload, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: You take two passengers on a flight with a cabin altitude of 15,500 feet MSL. What does 14 CFR 91.211 require for your passengers?
options: Each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen
Nothing, since only the required crew needs oxygen
Passengers need oxygen only after 30 minutes at that altitude
Passengers must use oxygen only above 18,000 feet
questions.why: Above 15,000 feet MSL cabin pressure altitude, each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]]. Above 14,000 feet, you as required crew must also use it the entire time at those altitudes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].

questions.q: Your engine fails low after takeoff, and a pilot is tempted to turn back to the runway. Even if the airplane makes it back, what extra problem does the AFH warn about?
options: The runway lights will be off
It always ends in a crosswind landing within limits
It often ends in a downwind landing, with higher groundspeed and more energy to absorb
The airplane will arrive too slow to flare
questions.why: A return to the airport often results in a downwind approach. The higher groundspeed can rush a pilot not trained to land downwind, and the extra groundspeed and energy raise the chance of serious injury if you can't make the field [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Doubling groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

questions.q: Emergency Autoland (EAL) is flying your airplane toward an airport after you became incapacitated. Then it loses GPS coverage. What does the AFH say it does?
options: It lands at the nearest airport using visual references
It keeps flying straight without trying to land until GPS coverage returns
It starts a slow spiral down over its present position
It turns toward the nearest VOR and lands there
questions.why: If the system loses GPS coverage, the airplane continues straight flight without attempting to land until GPS coverage resumes. EAL only considers airports with an RNAV or GPS approach [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
